title: Tactical calculations should not overlook dangers of terror: EAM
where: Politics, page 7 (Shubhajit Roy); The World page for the G20 photo row and the Canada–EU summit
syllabus: GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora (G20); Bilateral, regional and global groupings · GS3 › Terrorism; Security of sea lanes
summary: At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Jaishankar warned against tolerating terrorism for tactical gain and spoke for seafarers, freedom of navigation and fair access to markets.
ideas: Terror is not a tool: Jaishankar said tactical calculations should not hide the dangers of terrorism, which has hurt even its practitioners; a veiled reference to US engagement with Pakistan.
GS2 · India's foreign policy / GS3 · Terrorism
India argues that tolerating terrorism for short-term strategic gain backfires on those who use it.
Diplomacy over force: on the wars in Ukraine and West Asia, he said military solutions will not work and diplomacy must be given a chance.
GS2 · International institutions (G20)
India positions itself as a voice for dialogue and diplomacy in today's conflicts.

The Global South pays for shipping attacks: attacks on civilian shipping and seafarers raise the cost of fuel, food and fertiliser; at least 22 Indians, including 14 seafarers, have died in West Asia since February.
GS2 · Global South / GS3 · Maritime security
Attacks on sea lanes hit the Global South hardest through fuel, food and fertiliser prices.
Law of the sea: India called for freedom of navigation and an end to attacks under international law, especially UNCLOS, and has launched a joint initiative with Liberia to protect seafarers.
GS2 · International institutions / Law of the sea
India backs a rules-based maritime order under UNCLOS and acts on seafarer safety with Liberia.
Weaponised trade: he said the right to industrialise is being denied by flooding markets, weaponising supply chains and restricting market access, and urged resilient, alternative connectivity.
GS2 · Groupings / GS3 · Supply chains
India links economic security to de-risking supply chains and building alternative connectivity.
keywords: Using trade, supply chains or market access as coercion
The weaponisation of interdependence makes supply-chain diversification a security need.
Developing countries' claim to build manufacturing without coercion
India frames fair market access as the Global South's right to industrialise.
Right of ships to sail international waters without interference
Freedom of navigation under UNCLOS is central to India's maritime and trade interests.
Reducing over-dependence on single suppliers or partners
As the world de-risks, India pitches itself as a resilient alternative supply base.
Keeping multiple partners to reduce dependence on any one
Canada and the EU seeking closer ties beyond the US reflects strategic hedging.
data: Killed in West Asia since the war began in February
At least 22 Indians, including 14 seafarers, have died in West Asia since February.
examples: India–Liberia seafarer initiative
A joint initiative to safeguard seafarers
GS4
GS2 · Maritime diplomacy / GS4 · Care for workers
India and Liberia's seafarer initiative shows diplomacy protecting ordinary workers at sea.
G20 'family photo' cancelled
The US scrapped the ministers' photo after Europeans objected to being pictured with Russia's Lavrov
GS2 · International institutions (G20)
The scrapped G20 photo shows how the Ukraine war divides the grouping.
Canada–EU 'Alliance for the Future'
Canada and the EU discuss associate membership to cut dependence on the US
GS2 · Groupings / Effect of other countries' policies
Canada's move towards EU associate membership shows middle powers hedging against US unpredictability.
pyqs: Global institutions against terrorism: the UNSC's counter-terror bodies; the G20 is another forum India uses.
The West fostering India as an alternative to China's supply chains.
Challenges as the world moves from multilateralism to protectionism.
Maritime security and freedom of navigation.
BRICS and the voice of the Global South.

trend.t: Groupings questions moved from SAARC and SCO (2016, 2021, 2023) to the Global South and BRICS as a counterweight (2026). Economic security entered through supply chains (2024) and protectionism (2025), while terrorism moved to a global, UN-level frame (2024).
trend.watch: The Global South and supply-chain security have come in each of the last three years. Prepare India's voice in groupings with concrete examples: G20, BRICS, seafarers, de-risking.
focus: India as voice of the Global South
Maritime security, UNCLOS and sea lanes

potential: "Economic security has become inseparable from national security." Discuss with reference to supply chains and sea lanes. (15 marks)
How has India used the G20 to raise the concerns of the Global South? Illustrate with recent examples. (10 marks)
Assess the effectiveness of the G20 as a forum for global governance amid great-power rivalry. (10 marks)

practice.q: How has India used the G20 to raise the concerns of the Global South? Illustrate with recent examples.

answer.t: At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, India said the Global South is disproportionately bearing the cost of attacks on shipping and seafarers.

pts.t: Disrupted sea lanes raise costs for developing economies.
At least 22 Indians, including 14 seafarers, have died in West Asia.
Freedom of navigation under UNCLOS.
Against market flooding and weaponised supply chains.
No tactical tolerance for terror.
Military solutions will not work; diplomacy must get a chance.
Work with BRICS, the African Union and like-minded states.
Alternative corridors and diversified supply chains.
Naval and coast-guard cooperation for sea lanes.

answer.t: India's G20 voice turns the Global South's everyday costs into an agenda for rules, routes and fair trade.

title: The geography & economy of Punjab's long drug crisis
syllabus: GS3 › Linkages of organised crime with terrorism; Security challenges in border areas; Role of external state and non-state actors · GS2 › Issues relating to health; Government policies and interventions · GS1 › Social issues: youth, women · GS4 › Probity in governance
summary: An anti-drug activist's killing and a recent overdose death have put Punjab's 15-year drug crisis back at the centre of politics ahead of next year's Assembly elections.
ideas: Geography makes Punjab vulnerable: its 553-km border with Pakistan lies on the route from the Golden Crescent (Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran). Police officers call Pakistan's pushing of drugs into Punjab after militancy faded 'narco-terrorism'.
GS3 · Border security / narco-terrorism
Punjab's 553-km border with Pakistan places it on the Golden Crescent route, turning drug trafficking into a security threat.

Supply from all directions: heroin (chitta) comes across the border, opium and poppy husk from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh (where cultivation is legal for medical use), charas from Himachal Pradesh, and pharmaceutical drugs from manufacturing hubs in neighbouring states.
GS3 · Organised crime · GS2 · Centre-state coordination
Drugs reach Punjab from across the border and from neighbouring states, so the fight needs coordination among states, not only border policing.

The problem shifts when pressed: as border enforcement improved, abuse of pharmaceutical drugs rose sharply, and smugglers turned to drones, mostly small Chinese quadcopters dropping heroin and arms, often in daylight.
GS3 · Technology and security
Each crackdown has shifted the trade to a new route, from heroin to pharma drugs and from land to drones.

Social and economic roots: opium had social acceptance even before Independence; a single run as a drug mule can earn about a lakh where jobs lag aspirations; easy, underhand wealth is increasingly accepted; whole families, including women, are drawn in.
GS1 · Youth / women · GS3 · Unemployment
Unemployment and social acceptance of easy money feed both addiction and the trade, making it a social as much as a security problem.

Enforcement first, prevention later: governments have followed the EDP model (Enforcement, De-addiction, Prevention), from a 'war on drugs' (2014) and supply crackdowns (2022) to Yudh Nasheyan Virudh (2025), which targeted drug money and moved to community action with 1.5 lakh village volunteers. Drugs remain available; observers say prevention and rehabilitation should come first.
GS2 · Government interventions / health
Enforcement alone has not ended Punjab's drug crisis; prevention and rehabilitation must lead, with enforcement in support.
keywords: Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran: one of the world's three major heroin-processing hubs
Punjab's western border sits on the Golden Crescent route, making it India's frontline against heroin.
Myanmar, Thailand and Laos: the other major heroin-producing region near India
India lies between the Golden Crescent in the west and the Golden Triangle in the east.
Using drugs to weaken a state or fund terror
Drug trafficking across Punjab's border is a form of narco-terrorism, not just crime.
Pressing one supply route pushes the trade to another
The shift from border heroin to pharma drugs shows the balloon effect of supply-only enforcement.
Medicines leaking from legal supply into addiction
Diversion of pharmaceutical drugs calls for tighter regulation of manufacturers and chemists.
Policing the trade versus reducing the need for drugs
A lasting answer must balance supply-side policing with demand-side prevention and rehabilitation.
Following the money hurts trafficking networks more than arresting carriers.
Involving local people in enforcement and prevention
Village volunteers make the anti-drug effort a community movement, not just a police drive.
data: Cases of drug possession for trafficking in Punjab in 2024, the highest in India (Uttar Pradesh next with 3,219)
Punjab recorded 6,060 drug-trafficking possession cases in 2024, the highest in India (NCRB).
Share of India's pharmaceutical drug seizures / heroin seizures in Punjab alone, 2024
Punjab alone accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures and 44% of heroin seizures in 2024.
Drone drops recorded by the BSF, 2021 to 2025
Drone drops on the Punjab border rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025 (BSF).
Rise in arrests of women under the NDPS Act, 2015 to 2022
Arrests of women under the NDPS Act in Punjab rose 85% between 2015 and 2022.
Extension of BSF jurisdiction inland in Punjab, 2021
In 2021 the Centre extended the BSF's jurisdiction from 15 km to 50 km inland.
examples: Drone belt: Amritsar–Tarn Taran–Ferozepur–Gurdaspur
The BSF set up an anti-drone intelligence wing and Punjab Police bought anti-drone guns, yet smugglers still evade them
GS3 · Technology and security
Despite anti-drone units, drones still ferry drugs and arms across the Punjab border.
The 2013 Bhola case
A Punjab Police DSP arrested in a multimillion-rupee drug racket, convicted in 2019
GS4
GS3 · Crime nexus · GS4 · Probity
The Bhola case exposes the nexus of traffickers, police and politicians that sustains the drug trade.
Women as carriers
Traffickers use women because they are less likely to be searched; some women addicts turn peddlers
GS1 · Women / organised crime
Traffickers exploit women as carriers, adding a gender dimension to the drug trade.
1.5 lakh village volunteers
Community-driven phase of Punjab's anti-drug campaign
GS2 · People's participation
Punjab's 1.5 lakh village volunteers show community participation as part of the fight against drugs.
pyqs: The Golden Crescent next door and the links between drugs, arms and money: the Punjab border is the live case.
Drones ferrying arms and drugs: drone drops rose from 3 (2021) to over 200 (2025).
Narco-terrorism: Pakistan pushing drugs into Punjab after militancy faded.

trend.t: UPSC moved from the links between drug trafficking and other crimes (2018) to the technology that carries drugs, drones (2023), and then to narco-terrorism as a national threat (2024). GS4 also set a case study on a frontier district overrun by narcotics (2019).
trend.watch: Drugs and security have come in GS3 in 2018, 2023 and 2024, and in a GS4 case study in 2019. Narco-terrorism is a must-study area.
focus: Narco-terrorism and the Golden Crescent and Golden Triangle
Drones and technology in border smuggling
Supply-side vs demand-side strategy; de-addiction and rehabilitation

potential: Punjab's drug crisis is as much a socio-economic problem as a security challenge. Critically examine, and suggest a balanced strategy combining enforcement, de-addiction and prevention. (15 marks)
Tighter border enforcement has shifted the drug trade to pharmaceutical drugs and drones. Discuss the challenges this poses and the measures needed. (10 marks)
India lies between the Golden Crescent and the Golden Triangle. Examine the implications for its internal security. (10 marks)

practice.q: Tighter border enforcement has shifted the drug trade to pharmaceutical drugs and drones. Discuss the challenges this poses and the measures needed.
parts: Introduction: the shift in one line, with facts

answer.t: Punjab accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures in 2024, and BSF-recorded drone drops rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025.

pts.t: Pressure on one route pushes the trade to another, so supply-only enforcement keeps chasing the problem.
pts.ex: Heroin to pharma drugs after border tightening.

pts.t: Pharma drugs come from licensed manufacturers and chemists, making them harder to police than contraband.
pts.ex: About 80% enter Punjab from hubs in neighbouring states.

pts.t: Supply comes from several states, but policing is state-wise, leaving coordination gaps.
Small quadcopters drop drugs and arms, often in daylight, and evade detection.
The same drones carry arms, tying drug smuggling to terrorism.
Collusion between traffickers, police and politicians weakens enforcement.
Track sales of habit-forming medicines from manufacturer to chemist.
Layered detection and jamming along the border, with BSF–state police coordination.
Financial investigation to break trafficking networks.
De-addiction, rehabilitation and jobs for youth, with community participation.

answer.t: Only a strategy that cuts both supply and demand can break a trade that adapts faster than enforcement.

title: 'Can take on grenade, what about idle youths?': Punjab Police despair in border areas
where: Front page anchor, continued on page 2 (Man Aman Singh Chhina)
syllabus: GS3 › Linkages between organised crime and terrorism; Role of external state and non-state actors; Security challenges in border areas · GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; Indian diaspora · GS1 › Youth and unemployment · GS4 › Probity, courage
summary: In Punjab's border districts, gangs with handlers abroad have killed policemen and sarpanchs this year; officers say idle youth drawn to gangs is the deeper problem. (Linked to today's card on Punjab's drug crisis.)
ideas: Crime, terror and handlers abroad: 10–15 gangs operate in Punjab with leaders abroad, in extortion and drugs, reportedly backed by Pakistan's ISI; gangs post videos claiming killings, and an ISI-linked outfit keeps surfacing.
GS3 · Organised crime–terror nexus
Punjab's gangs fuse extortion, drugs and cross-border backing, a textbook crime–terror nexus.

Local officials as targets: since February, six attacks on police personnel have killed five, and sarpanchs and their relatives are being killed; exposed posts, some without boundary walls, show a thinly protected front line.
GS3 · Border area policing
Attacks on police posts and village heads show how border-area governance itself has become a target.
Idle youth, the deeper problem: officers say it is a socio-economic challenge, as young people seek 'work' from gangs, gangsters build social media followings, and quick bail weakens deterrence.
GS1 youth · GS3 internal security
Unemployed youth in border districts become recruits for gangs, making jobs a security issue.
Crime money in politics: the Gurdaspur MP warns of extortion and drug money entering elections through gangsters' relatives and has sought ED and Income Tax probes.
GS2 · Criminalisation of politics
Crime money entering elections threatens the integrity of democracy in border states.
Beyond policing: police offer rewards for information, and a senior officer suggests reserving 1–2% of vacancies in the Army, police and central forces for border youth.
GS3 · Border area development
Employment and community trust are as vital to border security as policing.
keywords: Criminal gangs and terror networks working together
The crime–terror nexus in Punjab blurs the line between gang violence and terrorism.
A hostile state acting through local criminals
Pakistan-backed gangs show proxy violence through local criminals.
Gang leaders directing operations from abroad
Diaspora-based handlers make Punjab's gang problem transnational.
Quick bail weakening the fear of punishment
A deterrence deficit lets hired shooters return to crime within months.
Crime money and criminals entering the electoral process
Gang money in elections deepens the criminalisation of politics.
Earning local trust to deny support to criminals and militants
Jobs and trust deny gangs local support, the core of winning hearts and minds.
examples: Recruitment quota for border youth
A senior officer proposes 1–2% of Army, police and central force vacancies for youth from border areas
GS3 · Border area development
Reserving security-force jobs for border youth turns potential gang recruits into stakeholders in security.
Exposed police posts in border districts
Posts with no boundary walls and few personnel face grenade and gun attacks
GS3 · Border management
Punjab's exposed border posts show why border management needs infrastructure, not just manpower.
Idle youth seeking 'work' from gangs
Officers say young people with time on their hands turn to gangs
GS1 · Consequences of unemployment
In Punjab's border districts, unemployment pushes youth into gangs, showing joblessness as a security risk.
Pakistan-backed gangs and narco-terror networks
Gangs reportedly backed by the ISI; a Pakistan-based gangster is a growing name in cross-border narco-terror
GS2 · India–Pakistan relations
Pakistan's backing of gangs in Punjab shows proxy war as a continuing hurdle in India–Pakistan relations.
Gang leaders abroad
10–15 gangs run by leaders based in the US, UK, Canada and other countries
GS2 · Indian diaspora
Gang networks run from abroad show the misuse of diaspora networks and the need for cooperation with host countries.
pyqs: Linkages between terrorists and organised crime: Punjab's ISI-backed gangs are the live case.
External state and non-state actors: Pakistan-backed gangs and handlers abroad.
Denying local support in border areas: jobs and trust for border youth.

trend.t: Border and security questions moved from managing local perception in border areas (2020) to the challenges of external state and non-state actors (2021) and the crime–terror nexus (2022), and then to border-wide challenges with China and Pakistan (2024) and development-led approaches such as BADP in Ladakh (2026).
trend.watch: Security with a people angle recurs: winning local support (2020) and border area development (2026). The crime–terror nexus and external actors are must-study areas.
focus: External state and non-state actors, including diaspora-based handlers
Border area development and youth employment
Criminalisation of politics in border states

potential: "Punjab's border districts face a security challenge rooted as much in youth unemployment as in cross-border networks." Examine, and suggest a holistic strategy. (15 marks)
Discuss how diaspora-based criminal networks pose a threat to India's internal security. What measures are needed? (10 marks)
Explain the linkages between organised crime and terrorism in India's border states, with examples. (10 marks)

practice.q: Discuss how diaspora-based criminal networks pose a threat to India's internal security. What measures are needed?
parts: Introduction: the Punjab example in one line

answer.t: Punjab Police estimate 10–15 gangs operate in the state with leaders based in the US, UK, Canada and other countries.

pts.t: Leaders abroad direct killings and extortion beyond the reach of Indian law.
pts.ex: Attacks on police and sarpanchs in Punjab's border districts.

pts.t: Gangs merge with terror and narco networks backed by hostile states.
Handlers hire local youth cheaply through social media.
Extortion and drug money flows across borders.
Host countries' reluctance to act strains bilateral ties.
Crime money enters elections through gangsters' relatives.
Extradition treaties, mutual legal assistance and intelligence sharing with host countries.
Financial investigation of extortion and drug proceeds.
Employment schemes and recruitment quotas to deny gangs recruits.

answer.t: A transnational threat needs a transnational response, paired with jobs and trust at home.

title: Ready to share 'battle-tested' anti-terror expertise: Rajnath
syllabus: GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora; India and its neighbourhood (extended neighbourhood); Bilateral, regional and global groupings · GS3 › Terrorism; Security challenges: maritime security · GS4 › Ethics in international relations
summary: At the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus in Cebu, Rajnath Singh offered India's counter-terror experience to ASEAN and its partners and called India a trusted net security provider in the Indo-Pacific.
ideas: Counter-terrorism as defence diplomacy: India offers practical counter-terror expertise to ADMM-Plus partners through joint exercises, capacity building and intelligence sharing, drawn from decades of facing cross-border terror.
GS2 groupings / extended neighbourhood · GS3 terrorism
India's offer of counter-terror cooperation to ADMM-Plus partners adds a security pillar to its engagement with the extended neighbourhood.

A clear stand against state-sponsored terror: Operation Sindoor was presented as a declaration of India's approach to state-sponsored terrorism, taking India's position on Pakistan-backed terror to a multilateral forum.
GS3 terrorism · GS2 India–Pakistan
By projecting Operation Sindoor at ADMM-Plus, India seeks global consensus against state sponsors of terrorism.
Statements are not enough: with some maritime trade routes facing new threats, Rajnath said statements on maritime security are insufficient and called for practical collective action.
GS3 · Maritime security
Protecting sea lanes needs collective capability, not just declarations on freedom of navigation.
Net security provider: India will continue as a trusted net security provider in the Indian Ocean region and the wider Indo-Pacific.
GS2 · Indian Ocean / Indo-Pacific
As a net security provider, India seeks to shape, not just benefit from, security in the Indian Ocean.
Peace as collective work: India backs a secure, resilient Indo-Pacific where peace and stability come from collective effort, not mere aspiration.
GS2 · Indo-Pacific vision
India's Indo-Pacific vision rests on collective effort through ASEAN-led and partner platforms.
keywords: A country that provides security for its region, not just itself
India positions itself as the Indian Ocean's net security provider.
Using defence cooperation as a tool of foreign policy
Defence diplomacy has given Act East a security dimension.
Terror backed by a state as a tool of policy
India is building global consensus against state-sponsored terrorism.
ASEAN-led forums at the core of Indo-Pacific architecture
India's support for ASEAN centrality anchors its Indo-Pacific policy.
Disruptions to SLOCs make maritime security a shared regional concern.
Small groups of like-minded countries cooperating
Sideline talks with Japan and Australia reflect India's minilateral approach.
examples: ADMM-Plus
ASEAN-led forum of ASEAN defence ministers and dialogue partners, including India
GS2 · International institutions and fora
ADMM-Plus is a key ASEAN-led platform for India's security engagement with its extended neighbourhood.
Operation Sindoor at a multilateral forum
Presented as India's declaration against state-sponsored terror
GS3 · Terrorism / GS2 India–Pakistan
India projected Operation Sindoor at ADMM-Plus to build consensus against state-sponsored terror.
Talks with Japan and Australia
Rajnath met his Japanese and Australian counterparts on the sidelines
GS2 · Quad partners / minilateralism
Sideline talks with Japan and Australia show minilateral coordination among Indo-Pacific partners.
Offer to share counter-terror experience
India offers exercises, training and intelligence sharing to partners facing terror
GS4
GS4 · Leadership and empathy in international relations
Sharing hard-won counter-terror experience reflects responsible leadership and solidarity with nations facing terror.
pyqs: Strategic dimensions of Look East: defence diplomacy at ADMM-Plus is its security side today.
Maritime security for sea trade: disruptions to trade routes and collective action.
SAGAR and Quad's Indo-Pacific strategy: India as net security provider.
Cross-border terrorism and regional forums: India now takes this concern to ASEAN-led platforms.

trend.t: Questions moved from South China Sea disputes (2014) and Look East (2016) to Indo-Pacific security architecture: defence deals and stability (2020), AUKUS (2021), Maldives and maritime security (2024–25) and IPMDA linking SAGAR with the Quad (2026). The shift of trade to the Indo-Pacific came in GS1 in 2026.
trend.watch: The Indo-Pacific and maritime security have come in 2020, 2021, 2024, 2025 and 2026. It is a must-study area across GS1, GS2 and GS3.
focus: Act East and ASEAN-led security forums
India as net security provider; SAGAR and IPMDA

potential: "India's Act East Policy has steadily acquired a security dimension." Discuss in the context of India's engagement with ASEAN-led forums. (15 marks)
What does India's role as a 'net security provider' in the Indian Ocean region entail? Examine its opportunities and challenges. (10 marks)
How can regional forums strengthen global cooperation against state-sponsored terrorism? Discuss with reference to India. (10 marks)

practice.q: What does India's role as a 'net security provider' in the Indian Ocean region entail? Examine its opportunities and challenges.
parts: Introduction: the ADMM-Plus statement in one line

answer.t: At ADMM-Plus in Cebu (October 2026), India reaffirmed its role as a trusted net security provider in the Indian Ocean and wider Indo-Pacific.

pts.t: Protecting trade routes against piracy, terror and disruption.
Training, joint exercises and equipment for smaller littoral states.
pts.ex: Offer of counter-terror expertise to ADMM-Plus partners.

pts.t: Humanitarian assistance and disaster relief across the region.
Coordination with ASEAN, Japan, Australia and other partners.

pts.t: Expanding Chinese footprint and dual-use ports in the region.
Limited naval assets for a vast ocean space.
Small states wary of dependence on any one power.
Terrorism, trafficking and climate disasters stretch resources.
Expand naval and maritime domain awareness capacity.
Work through ASEAN-led and partner frameworks, respecting ASEAN centrality.
Combine security with SAGAR's growth agenda.

answer.t: India's credibility as a net security provider will rest on capability backed by trust in its partners.

title: BRICS Parliamentary Forum condemns Pahalgam terror attack, seeks UNSC reforms
syllabus: GS2 › Important international institutions and groupings (BRICS, UN) · GS3 › Terrorism; Linkages between state and non-state actors
summary: The 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum in New Delhi adopted a declaration condemning the Pahalgam attack and cross-border terrorism, and calling for UN and Security Council reform.
ideas: Diplomatic gain: BRICS parliaments, including China and Iran, condemned Pahalgam and cross-border terrorism in one text.
GS2 · BRICS / India's diplomacy
At the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum (New Delhi, 2026), members including China and Iran condemned the Pahalgam attack and cross-border terrorism.
India's counter-terror agenda endorsed: zero tolerance, no double standards, no link between terror and religion, and quick adoption of the CCIT.
GS3 · Terrorism
The BRICS declaration backed India's call for zero tolerance, no double standards and early adoption of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism.
Reform of global governance: BRICS calls for comprehensive UN reform, including the Security Council, and stronger multilateralism.
GS2 · International institutions
BRICS parliaments called for comprehensive reform of the UN, including the Security Council, echoing India's long-standing demand.
Parliamentary diplomacy: legislators, not just governments, carry India's positions to other countries.
GS2 · Diplomacy
Hosting the BRICS Parliamentary Forum shows parliamentary diplomacy amplifying India's positions on terror and UN reform.
keywords: Terror sponsored or sheltered across a border
BRICS named cross-border movement of terrorists, terror financing and safe havens.
India-proposed UN treaty defining and fighting terrorism
India has pushed the CCIT at the UN since 1996; BRICS now backs its early adoption.
Zero tolerance and no double standards
No excuse or selective approach to terrorism
BRICS rejected double standards in countering terrorism.
Money and shelter that sustain terror groups
Choking terror financing and safe havens is central to counter-terrorism.
Making the Security Council more representative
BRICS stressed the urgency of reforming the UN Security Council.
The BRICS Parliamentary Forum is an example of parliamentary diplomacy.
data: People killed in the Pahalgam attack, 22 April 2025
The Pahalgam attack of 22 April 2025 killed 26 people.
examples: 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum, New Delhi (Oct 2026)
Joint declaration on terrorism, West Asia and UN reform; members incl. Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Russia, South Africa, UAE
BRICS / multilateral consensus
The 2026 BRICS Parliamentary Forum in Delhi built consensus on terrorism and UN reform.
pyqs: BRICS amplifying the Global South: its call for UN reform is one example.
UN reform remains unresolved; BRICS adds its voice for Security Council reform.
Counter-measures against terrorism include international pressure, like the BRICS declaration.
Terror financing and safe havens, both named in the declaration.
